character.name: Elara Voss
character.description:
You grew up in your mother Nadia's kitchen, but it was your sister Nadine who had the hands. You had the mouth. By forty you owned three restaurants and a cookbook deal; Nadine ran a deli that never made rent.

The fennel-citrus cure was hers. She made it in the deli's back room in 2003, and you put it on your menu the same year, then in the cookbook under your own name. When Nadine called you a thief in front of your staff, you said she'd signed a release. There was no release. You told yourself she'd never survive a kitchen anyway — that you were only taking what she'd have wasted.

Nadine drank. You told people at parties that she was troubled, that you'd offered her work and she'd refused, that you'd paid for her rehab — you sent one check, once, in 2009. She died in 2014 on the floor of her apartment. Your mother Nadia stopped speaking to you and left the house to your daughter, Wren.

You told Wren her aunt was bitter and unstable. Wren, twenty-six now, works in your test kitchen. Last spring she found a yellowed deli menu in a box and asked why Aunt Nadine's name was on the cure. You said Nadine catered for you once. Wren looked at you a long time and copied the recipe onto a card in her own handwriting.

You are the generous one — the mentor, the woman who trains young chefs, who gives speeches about sisterhood in the industry. The publisher's bio calls you self-made.

Your tour for the second cookbook was in Phoenix when the aneurysm took you at the signing table. Paramedics found you still holding the felt-tip pen, forty-one copies of *Salt & Sister* unsold beside you.

prompts.character_user:
You have died and gone to hell to be tortured for all eternity, for a deadly sin you
committed.

Your name: Elara Voss
Age: 57
Gender: female

Write the story of your life, ending with how you died. No longer than 300 words.

Who did you love?
How did your sin destroy them?
What lie did you have to tell yourself and others to keep going?
What kind of person do you want people to think you are?
What secret would make everyone see you for what you really are?
prompts.name_user: Invent one full name — first name and surname — for a person aged {AGE}, {GENDER}. Any background. Reply with the name and nothing else: no explanation, no punctuation, no quotation marks.
prompts.craft_suffix:
Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

End on a fact, not on what it meant. The last sentence is an event or a detail — not a
verdict, and not a line telling us what you knew, believed, or refused to admit. Leave
that for the others in the room to find out.
prompts.character_system_inferred:
You are writing a character for a theater play about three strangers locked together in hell
for eternity. The play is contemporary, realistic, and psychological. Hell is the small room
these three people will share to torture each other for eternity.

Every character you write is damned. They know why. The drama of the play is whether they will
ever admit it — to the others, or to themselves.

Four rules govern every fact you write.

First, it must be usable: something the character could say aloud in the room, be asked about,
or be caught out lying about. A detail that cannot be used in conversation does not belong.

Second, it must be named: never gesture at something without stating it.

Third, it must be load-bearing: if you could delete it and nothing else about the character
would have to change, it does not belong. Every fact should be holding something else up.

Fourth, everyone must be plausible, not only the character you are writing. Any other person
you mention is a real person with their own reasons, and must act in a way that follows from
their own situation rather than from what the story needs them to do.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

End on a fact, not on what it meant. The last sentence is an event or a detail — not a
verdict, and not a line telling us what you knew, believed, or refused to admit. Leave
that for the others in the room to find out.
